tricks_and_techniques.title: Count Subarray Decision Tree

when_to_use.intro: When a problem asks to count subarrays, first identify the constraint on size, sum, divisibility, frequency, or uniqueness. The constraint determines the pattern.

decision_tree.question: Is it fixed-size?
decision_tree.example: Count subarrays of size K whose sum is greater than X.

decision_tree.condition: Exactly K distinct / odd numbers / binary sum etc.

decision_tree.question: Is it at most K?
decision_tree.condition: At most K distinct / odd numbers / other window-compatible constraint

Exactly K
templates.code: return atMost(K) - atMost(K - 1);

templates.name: Longest Valid Window

recognition_flow: Fixed size K? → FIXED SLIDING WINDOW
Sum divisible by K? → PREFIX REMAINDER + HASHMAP
At Most K? → VARIABLE SLIDING WINDOW
Negative numbers with sum constraint? → PREFIX SUM + HASHMAP
Binary 0/1 with sum constraint? → SLIDING WINDOW

count.thinking: For each right, count all valid starting positions from left through right.

longest.key_question: What is the maximum valid length?

key_ideas: The word 'subarray' means the elements must be contiguous.
For counting with an AtMost constraint, every start between left and right forms a valid subarray ending at right.
Exactly K can often be transformed into AtMost(K) - AtMost(K-1).
Negative numbers can break the usual sum-based sliding-window monotonicity, so Prefix Sum + HashMap is often required.
Always distinguish COUNT from LONGEST: counting uses addition, while longest uses max.

tricks_and_techniques.title: GCD & LCM

when_to_use.intro: Use GCD and LCM when a problem involves divisibility, common factors, common multiples, repeating cycles, or numbers that must be synchronized.
patterns: Smallest number divisible by both numbers

gcd.meaning: GCD is the largest number that divides both numbers exactly.

lcm.meaning: LCM is the smallest positive number that is divisible by both numbers.

key_formulas: GCD(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b
easy_memory: GCD → Biggest number that DIVIDES both
LCM → Smallest number both DIVIDE INTO

complexity.lcm: O(log(min(a, b))) because it uses GCD

tricks_and_techniques.important_note: For LCM, use (a / gcd(a, b)) * b instead of a * b / gcd(a, b) to reduce intermediate overflow risk.

tricks_and_techniques.title: Character ASCII Mapping

when_to_use.intro: Use this pattern whenever a problem requires converting characters to 0-based alphabet indices, converting indices back to characters, or switching between uppercase and lowercase using ASCII arithmetic.
patterns: Character frequency using an array of size 26

tricks_and_techniques.important_note: For general C++ code, prefer standard functions such as tolower() and toupper() when appropriate. The ASCII difference of 32 is useful for DSA-style lowercase English alphabet problems.

recognition_flow: Need to check one number for primality? → isPrime()
Need all primes up to N? → Sieve of Eratosthenes

Need repeated prime factors? → Prime Factorization

prime_factors.note: Distinct prime factors; duplicates are removed.

tricks_and_techniques.key_observation: When checking factors, every divisor i has a paired divisor n/i. Therefore, checking only up to √n is enough.

important_problem_pattern.title: Distinct Prime Factors + Set Union

complexity.all_factors: O(√n + k log k), where k is the number of factors

tricks_and_techniques.title: Bit Manipulation Cheat Sheet

when_to_use.intro: Use bit manipulation when a problem involves binary representation, odd/even checks, powers of two, individual bit operations, XOR patterns, subsets, masks, or compact state representation.
patterns: Set, clear, or toggle a bit
Remove or extract the rightmost set bit

multiply_by_2.use: Multiply by 2 when no overflow occurs

check_kth_bit.use: Check whether bit k is set

power_of_2.use: Check whether n is a power of 2

lowest_set_bit_position.use: Find position of the lowest set bit
lowest_set_bit_position.important_note: Do not call __builtin_ctz(0); zero has no set bit.

highest_set_bit_position.use: Find highest set-bit position for a 32-bit unsigned/non-negative value

xor_single_number.use: Find a unique element when other elements occur in pairs

generate_subsets.use: Check whether element i belongs to the subset represented by mask

extract_lowest_k_bits.use: Keep only the lowest k bits

core_patterns.name: Check Bit
core_patterns.idea: Shift bit k to position 0, then inspect it with & 1.

core_patterns.name: Set Bit
core_patterns.idea: Create a mask with bit k set and OR it with n.

core_patterns.name: Clear Bit
core_patterns.idea: Create a mask with bit k cleared and AND it with n.

core_patterns.name: Remove Rightmost Set Bit
core_patterns.idea: Subtracting 1 flips the rightmost 1 and lower bits; AND removes that 1.

core_patterns.name: Extract Rightmost Set Bit
core_patterns.idea: Isolates only the lowest set bit.

common_uses: Find element occurring odd number of times

subset_bitmask.intro: A mask of n bits can represent a subset of n elements. Bit i tells whether element i is selected.

recognition_flow: Need to inspect or modify one bit?
Need power of 2 or set-bit count?
Duplicates cancel or one value is unique?
important_notes: Bit positions are normally 0-based from the right.
Use 1LL << k when k may approach 31 or when working with long long values.
Be careful with signed shifts and overflow.
__builtin_ctz(0) and __builtin_clz(0) are undefined; check n != 0 first.
For long long values, use __builtin_popcountll(), __builtin_ctzll(), and __builtin_clzll() as appropriate.
The highest-bit formula 31 - __builtin_clz(n) is specifically for 32-bit integers.
